title: Dissipation Enables Strongly Detuning-Dependent Interference in Pulsed Dynamical Decoupling
authors: Kenneth DeRose, Jonah Glick, Kefeng Jiang, Hans Johnson, Tanay Roy, Sharika Saraf, Anya Abraham, Hardeep Singh, Tim Kovachy
abstract: One of the defining features of pulsed dynamical decoupling is its suppression of a driven qubit's sensitivity to static detuning errors between the drive field and qubit resonance. In this paper, we show that dissipation, in the form of excited-state decay, can change this behavior entirely, producing an interference signal with a strong detuning dependence. This signal arises from decay during driven evolution and relies on coherence retained by the qubit after such a decay event. We develop analytical and numerical models that capture the underlying mechanism and observe this same dissipation-induced detuning dependence experimentally in both a free-space strontium atom interferometer and a superconducting transmon qubit system. We also use this dissipation-induced detuning dependence as the basis for a new spectroscopic technique called Dissipative Carr-Purcell Spectroscopy (DCPS) and compare it with a traditional Ramsey sequence. Our results establish a regime of pulsed dynamical decoupling in which dissipation reshapes, rather than merely degrades, coherent control, and we expect these dynamics to be relevant to a wide range of quantum systems.
summary: The paper demonstrates that spontaneous decay during pulsed dynamical decoupling sequences fundamentally changes the expected behavior, introducing a strong dependence on detuning. This effect is modeled analytically and experimentally verified using both strontium atoms and transmon qubits. The findings establish Dissipative Carr-Purcell Spectroscopy (DCPS) as a new tool for quantum characterization.
main_problem: Investigating how spontaneous dissipation (excited-state decay) fundamentally alters the behavior of pulsed dynamical decoupling sequences, potentially creating a strong detuning dependence where none existed before.
main_result: Dissipation can reshape coherent control in DD sequences, causing the system to exhibit a measurable interference signal whose phase and visibility are strongly dependent on the detuning from resonance.
method: The study uses analytical and numerical modeling of driven two-level systems, validated by experimental measurements on both strontium atoms and superconducting transmon qubits.
model_or_system: The core model is a driven two-level system qubit subjected to pulsed dynamical decoupling sequences (like Carr-Purcell). The physical platforms include free-space strontium atom interferometers and superconducting transmon qubits, both exhibiting relaxation ($T_1$).
key_observables: Phase shift ($\Delta\phi$), Visibility ($v$), and the detuning dependence of these quantities.
important_parameters: Detuning ($\delta$) relative to resonance, decay rate ($\gamma = 1/T_1$), and pulse timings (e.g., $	au_\pi$, $T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on first-order approximations in detuning error ($\delta$) and requires explicit correction factors for decay occurring during the final detection readout.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the gate-based impact of relaxation, Bloch sphere trajectories showing state distributions after decay (arcs), and measured $\Delta\phi$ and $v$ versus normalized detuning ($\delta/\Omega$) for both atomic and superconducting systems.
paper_structure: The paper moves from establishing the theoretical mechanism of dissipation altering DD control to developing a new spectroscopic technique (DCPS) and finally presenting comparative experimental results across two distinct physical platforms.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it shows that open system dynamics (dissipation) can be harnessed not just as noise, but as a source of measurable quantum information, leading to novel spectroscopy techniques for characterizing coherence in complex systems.
